cards.body: European real estate investor SWI has launched its new AI cloud division, SWI Compute. SWI said its new compute division is supported by 3.6GW of power capacity across 24 sites in the US and Europe that the wider group has secured. SWI Compute will deploy globally, with a focus on Europe. Its first large-scale deployment will be located in Cambridge, UK. Starting with 30MW and hosting close to 7,000 Rubin GPUs and 3,500 Vera CPUs in Nvidia Vera Rubin NVL72 racks, the site expected to come online by the end of 2027. This 30MW is the initial phase of a UK campus planned to grow to 530MW, with the company targeting 2.3GW of Nvidia-focused capacity by 2029. Nvidia became a Preferred Nvidia Cloud Partner in August, ordering approximately $1 billion of Nvidia systems. The firm said it has finalized contracts with its first customers. "Energy availability represents the primary bottleneck facing European AI infrastructure. Having spent six years acquiring grid access, SWI Group is now deploying these power resources into dedicated Nvidia AI factories through SWI Compute," said Halil Mirakhmedov, CEO, SWI Compute. “Just two months after joining the Nvidia Cloud Partner program, our team secured approximately $1 billion in advanced hardware orders and executed initial client contracts. The market continues to surpass available capacity, and we are rapidly expanding our footprint to fulfill this requirement.” SWI added that every SWI Compute site is built to Nvidia reference architectures, and going forward will be designed, built, and operated to Nvidia’s DSX AI Factory Platform requirements. "AI factories are essential infrastructure that turn regional energy into intelligence and economic opportunity," said Nico Caprez, Vice President, global AI infrastructure growth at Nvidia. "SWI Compute is putting Europe's energy to work for the ecosystem of AI natives, labs, universities, and enterprises. Built on Nvidia reference architectures and adopting Nvidia DSX for its next generation of AI factories, SWI Compute is building infrastructure that is productive, durable, and fungible – able to serve new customers and workloads and keep generating value for years to come." Formed from the merger of Stoneweg and Icona Capital last year, Euronext Amsterdam SWI Group has some €11 billion ($12.27bn) in assets under management. The firm last year announced it was launching its own data center fund and platform, taking a stake in AiOnX, which has projects across the UK, Ireland, and mainland Europe. AiOnX is developing a data center park in Cambridge, UK, and near Dublin in Ireland. The company also lists projects in Milan, Italy; Varde, Denmark; and Madrid, Spain. The Irish site is reportedly leased to Amazon. Plans for SWI to launch a GPU-as-a-service provider were announced over the summer, though few details had been shared. The company was previously set to invest in German cloud and data center firm Polarise, but backed out to instead merely provide financing. I

cards.body: High-performance computing company Bull has been awarded a €40 million ($45m) contract with DKRZ, the German Climate Computing Center, to deliver the High-performance Computing System for the Earth System Research (HLRE-5) supercomputer. The system is expected to come online in early 2028, with the contract set to run for five years and include support services. Once live, the HLRE-5 will support both physics-based simulations as well as AI-driven climate research, DKRZ said in a statement, adding that the system will reduce the energy required per simulated year by around 75 percent when compared to the center’s current supercomputer, Levante. When it comes to HLRE-5, the XH3500-based supercomputer will comprise two partitions, a GPU partition powered by Nvidia GB200 Superchips, and a CPU partition containing Nvidia Vera CPUs, and use direct liquid cooling technology. The nodes will be interconnected by Nvidia Quantum-2 InfiniBand networking, while the storage is IBM Storage Scale System 6000, combining 60PB of high-capacity disk drive storage with up to 340 Gbps throughput and a dedicated 500TB flash tier. A district heating system will allow DKRZ to use the waste heat from the system to heat the University of Hamburg. “The new system will allow us to drastically reduce the energy needed for our users’ climate simulations," said Dr. Hendryk Bockelmann, head of DKRZ’s applications department. "For a center that exists to study the climate, that is not a side benefit – it is part of the job." Dr. Martin Matzke, head of Northern and Central Europe, Bull, added: “We are proud to continue our long-standing collaboration with DKRZ, one of Europe’s leading climate computing centers. HLRE-5 builds on years of joint innovation in energy-efficient supercomputing and demonstrates how advanced digital infrastructure can support excellent climate research." The contract award comes six months after the French state completed its acquisition of Bull, the former HPC and quantum subsidiary of Atos, following the signing of a €404m ($469m) share purchase agreement between Atos and the French State in July 2025. Its BullSequana HPC systems form the basis for a number of the world’s most powerful supercomputers, with its X series architecture supporting exascale-class systems, including Europe’s first exascale system, the Jupiter Booster. In April 2026, Bull revealed it had secured a €30 million ($35m) five-year contract to provide AI-optimized infrastructure at Sweden’s Mimer AI factory, also based on Bull’s BullSequana XH3500 architecture. Also this year, Bull was selected by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking (EuroHPC JU) and the Lumi AI factory consortium to deliver the Lumi-AI supercomputer, to be hosted at the CSC data center in Kajaani, Finland, and was separately awarded a €31 million ($36m) contract with the Spanish State Meteorological Agency (AEMET) to deliver supercomputing infrastructure.

cards.body: Forum Markets is to supply Nvidia-backed inference provider Fireworks with data center capacity in Texas. The Nasdaq-listed company this week announced that Forum Edge AI LLC, the company's joint venture (JV) with Edge Node Inc., has entered into a definitive agreement with Fireworks for a 36-month reservation of Nvidia B300 GPU capacity at its existing, powered data center facility in Dallas. The deal, Forum Edge's first contracted customer commitment, is valued at $94.4 million. The GPUs are expected to be deployed at Forum Edge's Dallas data center in late December or early January. "This agreement is an important proof point for our AI infrastructure strategy and reflects our focus on bringing revenue-generating GPUs to market quickly in a modular manner," said McAndrew Rudisill, Forum Markets chairman and CEO. "We have a strong partnership with Fireworks and are excited about our growth trajectory as we scale our AI infrastructure business. This is the first finalized contract Forum Edge is executing against and the first of several exciting partnerships we expect to deploy into our unique footprint." Founded in 2022, Fireworks provides inference, training, and routing that help enterprises deploy and scale generative AI applications in production. The company was most recently valued at approximately $17.5 billion, with backers including Nvidia, Atreides Management, Index Ventures, and TCV. The company rents GPU servers from other sources, and then sells access to open-source AI models, competing with the likes of Together AI and Baseten. Last year, Oracle revealed that it counts Fireworks AI among its customers. The company also uses GPUs from Voltage Park. On its website, Fireworks says it operates across 30 global regions across Europe, North America, and Asia Pacific. Investment firm Forum Markets announced a partnership with Edge Node Inc. earlier this month. The JV initial portfolio consists of 2MW of a 4MW data center in Dallas; a 9MW data center campus in High Point, North Carolina; and one initial mobile communications tower site of 1-2MW. Full details haven't been shared, but the Dallas data center currently offers 2MW, operated by Edge Node AI, with another 2MW coming later this year or early next year and allocated to the joint venture. Forum Markets is an asset manager that was previously focused on “tokenization of institutional-grade real-world assets on Ethereum.” Today the firm describes itself as investing in cash-generating assets across AI infrastructure, commercial aerospace, manufactured housing finance, and auto credit. Founded last year, Texas-based Edge Node is a ‘Tokens-as-a-Service’ provider, aiming to offer low-latency compute and inference services and access to LLMs in the US. The company has yet to launch its services.

cards.body: HPC Cadence, Nvidia Unveil New AI Models To Put EDA On Autopilot Like a virus, generative AI has invaded nearly every facet of technology, including chip and system design. If you ask Cadence Systems senior VP Paul Cunningham, somewhere between 20 and 30 percent of chips under development today are being designed with the help of AI agents, and that number is growing rapidly. In many ways, Cadence's latest products are among the clearest examples of how generative AI and HPC will coexist not just in industry but the sciences as well. Over the past year or so, the EDA giant has rolled out a series of so-called "AI Super Agents," including AuraStack for advanced packaging and PCB layout, ChipStack for SoC design and verification, InnoStack for PHY routing, and ViraStack for analog circuit design. Much like Anthropic's Claude Code or OpenAI's Codex, these harnesses are designed to work with LLMs to automate design and testing flows by orchestrating Cadence's existing EDA, test, and verification tools. This works for much the same reason that AI code assistants have exploded in popularity among software engineers. Code either compiles or it doesn't. Similarly, Cadence has tests to verify and validate its designs will work as intended. But just like many code assistants, the effectiveness of these tests depends heavily on how closely their training data resembles the inputs and outputs they're fed. Cadence's early agents were largely powered by off-the-shelf LLMs, which limited exposure to something like RTL. “It’s not the case that these amazingly powerful out-of-the-box foundation models are just going to do everything. They’re the starting point, and you can still specialize,” Cunningham said. In a bid for greater specialization, this week Cadence announced a partnership with Nvidia and launched its Maestro AI model family. These models were fine-tuned on Nvidia's Nemotron family of models to work with and interpret the results of Cadence's own tools. Not surprisingly, better domain knowledge tends to translate into better results. If Cadence is to be believed, early testing of its Maestro models showed an "up to" 30 percent increase in output quality and "up to" 5x greater token efficiency versus general purpose foundation models. In other words, post-trained models on Cadence's tools made them both smarter and cheaper to run. Along with the models, Cadence's Maestro platform also allows for customization based on customer data, although Cunningham tells us this will be offered more as managed service than something customers figure out on their own. Much like its existing agent harness, Cadence's Maestro models and agents can access the models via API, run in a secure VPC, or assuming you've got the hardware necessary, on prem. Cadence isn't the only one exploring the use of AI agents to orchestrate HPC workloads. headlines.body: BlackBerry CEO John Giamatteo sees artificial intelligence-powered robots as a major growth opportunity for the former smartphone king. Once one of the world's biggest mobile phone makers, Canada-based BlackBerry has reinvented itself. The company's QNX operating system, which provides underlying software for features ranging from braking systems to some semi-autonomous driving functions, is now embedded in more than 275 million vehicles worldwide. But the company is increasingly looking beyond the automotive industry to capitalize on the emerging market for physical AI. "While the products we sell today can't be held in the palm of your hand, they're pervasive around you," Giamatteo told CNBC's Jim Cramer on Monday. "275 million cars, robots, governments, medical instrumentation, supply chain. That's the new BlackBerry, and that's what's driving all of our growth." Robotics has already emerged as one of the fastest-growing businesses within QNX, according to Giamatteo. Unlike generative AI, which produces text and images, physical AI allows robots and other machines to interact with the real world. BlackBerry sees an opportunity to provide the underlying software that helps those machines operate safely and reliably, building on its experience in the automotive industry. That opportunity is contributing to BlackBerry's growing backlog. The company recently announced that its QNX royalty backlog surpassed $1.2 billion, increasing by more than $250 million over two quarters. Giamatteo identified three drivers behind that growth: automakers' transition to more advanced computing systems, expanded software offerings, and emerging demand for physical AI applications. Investors have taken notice of the turnaround. BlackBerry shares have surged 142% in 2026, following years of struggles for a company whose formerly ubiquitous handhelds with physical keyboards ruled the smartphone world before Apple's iPhone and other devices that were fully touchscreen. Back then called Research in Motion, the stock saw its market cap peak at nearly $85 billion in 2008, a year after the first iPhone. BlackBerry's current market cap is about $5.4 billion. Giamatteo also highlighted BlackBerry's partnership with Nvidia, which began in the automotive sector. Nvidia has now "standardized on QNX as the platform of choice" for its Halos Safety Stack, Giamatteo said. "That has opened up so many doors, an incredible pipeline of opportunity, and these are things like AMRs (automated mobile robots), autonomous forklifts, skateboards that are driving pallets to the docking station." headlines.body: COMPUTE Nvidia Simulates Its Way Into Google's Magic State Cultivation Party There’s a lot of innovation happening in the quantum computing field as it moves closer to the promised land of practical, scalable fault-tolerant systems. That said, reducing errors in calculations remains a core challenge that needs to be solved. Qubits are extremely fragile, can easily fall apart and lose their coherence, and a quantum system that makes too many errors is not useful. Quantum computing vendors create logical qubits from a collection of many physical qubits that can detect, isolate, and fix errors without interrupting the underlying quantum state. But it’s difficult to scale quantum systems when a single logical qubit could require thousands of physical qubits. And the scalability difficulties don't end there. Universal quantum systems – those that can run all operations already performed by classical servers plus those specific to quantum computers – need to include both Clifford gates (like S and CNOT gates) and non-Clifford gates (like T gates) to perform quantum algorithms. Most error correction codes can handle Clifford states, but not non-Clifford gates. In 2004, researchers introduced magic gates, which are prepared by the computer and injected into the computation. They are key to universal quantum computation, but they're also fragile, difficult to create with high fidelity, and can't be used again, so more have to be continuously created. Magic state distillation was used to offset this by collecting many noisy – or inaccurate – states and turning them into fewer, high-fidelity magic states. However, doing all of this takes time and can consume as much as 95 percent of a quantum system's capacity, creating a troubling resource bottleneck. Google researchers in 2024 introduced another technique – magic state cultivation – to more cheaply and efficiently generate high-fidelity magic states. Rather than create huge numbers of noisy states and then discard a lot of them, with cultivation, engineers can put a noisy state into a small area on the quantum chip and then – like a filter – run measurements via special coding techniques to find errors and remove flawed tries, eventually growing a lower-error magic state and significantly driving down the hardware overhead needed to run quantum algorithms. Putting Cultivation to Test On October 15, both Google and Nvidia announced projects they say significantly advance the development of magic state cultivation, with Google Quantum AI researchers reporting the first hardware implementation of the method. action.timeline: 1δ는 2027년 하반기 양산 예정, 1ε 이후 세대는 미확인
action.scope: Micron DRAM 공정 전 세대(1γ~ηÅ) 및 vHBM·vEIM 제품군, 고객사는 미확인

key_facts: Micron의 현행 1γ 공정은 양산 중이며, 후속 1δ는 2027년 하반기 양산 진입 예정이고 **비트 밀도 20%대 중반 향상**을 목표로 함
1δ는 HBM5, vHBM, vEIM 등 미래 AI 메모리 제품에 최적화됨
1ε부터 웨이퍼 본딩 도입 예정이나 구체적 구현 방식과 기대 효과는 미공개

**vEIM 1세대는 2TB/s 대역폭, <1pJ/bit 에너지**를 목표로 하며 이는 HBM4(8GT/s, 2,048비트 인터페이스) 수준과 동급
summary_data.why_matters: DRAM이 원자 단위 한계에 근접함에 따라 **메모리 업체 간 3D 적층·신공정 경쟁이 본격화**되며, 이는 AI 가속기의 메모리 대역폭·용량·전력 효율을 좌우하는 핵심 변수가 된다. 특히 프로세서 위에 직접 메모리를 쌓는 vHBM/vEIM 방식은 향후 AI GPU 및 엣지 AI 칩 설계 패러다임에 영향을 줄 수 있다.
summary_data.subject_angle: NVIDIA는 HBM 기반 AI GPU의 최대 고객사로서 Micron의 **vHBM 로드맵(프로세서 상단 적층, 저지연·고대역폭)**이 향후 AI 가속기 설계에 직접 영향을 미칠 수 있으며, HBM5 및 차세대 DRAM 공급 안정성과 성능 향상이 NVIDIA의 GPU 로드맵과 긴밀히 맞물린다.
summary_data.focus_angle: vEIM(vertical edge inference memory)은 **자율주행차·로봇 등 전력 제약 엣지 AI 프로세서**를 명시적 타깃으로 하며, 2TB/s 대역폭·<1pJ/bit 에너지 효율을 목표로 하여 NVIDIA의 자동차(DRIVE)·로봇(Jetson, Isaac 등) 플랫폼용 차세대 메모리 공급 가능성과 연결된다.

headlines.body: Having jettisoned 4F 2 memory cells from its roadmap , Micron must use different methods to continue scaling its DRAM devices in the coming years to keep up with rivals planning to use smaller DRAM transistors towards the end of the decade. Instead, Micron intends to introduce wafer bonding with its upcoming 1ε DRAM process technology and adopt High-NA EUV lithography for subsequent generations. Meanwhile, the company is developing new types of memory, including vertical high-bandwidth memory (vHBM) and vertical edge inference memory (vEIM), which will be integrated directly on top of processors. Tom's Hardware Premium Roadmaps (Image credit: Future) Leading-edge foundry roadmaps Nvidia Enterprise GPU and CPU roadmap AMD's Enterprise GPU and CPU roadmap Intel's roadmaps examined — 14A, Nova Lake, Diamond Rapids & AI accelerator push Co-Packaged Optics (CPO) foundry roadmaps "DRAM is nearing atomic limits at this point," said Scott DeBoer, president and chief technology and products officer at Micron, during the company's event this week. "Although we have confidence in several more planar nodes, we are very focused on making sure that we introduce 3D DRAM at the optimal time from a cost and performance point of view." Wafer bonding, High-NA EUV, and new materials Micron's current 1γ DRAM process is already in high-volume manufacturing, whereas its successor, 1δ, is scheduled to enter volume production in the second half of 2027. The latter promises a mid-20% increase in bit density and is optimized for future AI memory products, including HBM5, vHBM, and vEIM. Beyond 1δ, Micron plans to introduce wafer bonding with its 1ε process, which is currently under development. However, the company has not disclosed how it intends to implement wafer bonding or what improvements it expects from the technology. (Image credit: Micron) For subsequent generations — ζÅ and ηÅ — Micron plans to adopt High-NA EUV lithography (ζÅ, zeta angstrom, Micron's 1 st Generation sub-10nm-class DRAM node) and new materials (ηÅ, eta angstrom, Micron's 2 nd Generation sub-10nm-class DRAM node) to continue shrinking DRAM cells. For many of its upcoming fabrication technologies that will be used over the next five to 10 years, Micron is also collaborating with Albany NanoTech. Of course, as with all organizations like Albany NanoTech, we are mostly talking about fundamental, or pre-competitive, IP that could be used for DRAM production at some point. related.title: Cadence unveils Nvidia-powered AI data center in Munich, Germany

headlines.body: Cadence has launched a sovereign AI data center in Munich, Germany, that supports the company’s OnCloud and Reality Digital Twin platforms, alongside the Cadence Millennium M2000 AI Supercomputer. Powered by Nvidia Vera and Grace CPUs and Blackwell GPUs, Cadence said the data center provides “secure, European sovereign cloud infrastructure” for electronic design automation (EDA), simulation, and AI workloads. The facility is certified to ISO 27001, ISO 27017, and SOC 2 Type II standards, and will expand Cadence's European cloud footprint. The data center will complement existing European cloud resources, including leading public cloud provider infrastructure in Frankfurt. The company’s Reality Digital Twin platform allows customers to design, validate, and optimize next-generation AI infrastructure before deployment, with Cadence stating it will use the platform within the Munich facility to improve the design and operation of its compute infrastructure, boost energy efficiency, and reduce operational risk. “Europe's semiconductor and system design community requires secure infrastructure that enables innovation without compromising data sovereignty,” said Paul Scannell, SVP of the global customer success team at Cadence. “By combining Nvidia Vera and Grace CPU platforms with the Cadence Millennium M2000 Supercomputer and making these capabilities available through Cadence OnCloud, we are providing European engineering teams with the compute, design intelligence and flexibility needed to build the next generation of AI-driven chips and systems.” “Chip designs and AI infrastructure are strategic assets for European industry, and sovereignty means being able to develop both while protecting the data behind them,” said Tim Costa, VP and GM of industrial and computational engineering at Nvidia. “With Cadence, we’re bringing NVIDIA accelerated computing into European cloud-based design workflows and Omniverse libraries into AI factory simulation. Companies can design the silicon and validate the infrastructure to run it – from power delivery to cooling – within a European environment built to protect their design data.” Cadence OnCloud on sovereign infrastructure is available today to European customers, with additional compute capabilities, including Nvidia Vera and Grace and CPU systems, the Cadence Millennium M2000 AI Supercomputer, and Cadence Reality Digital Twin Platform instances, planned as part of the ongoing expansion of the Munich data center.

headlines.body: Karman has deployed its AI-enabled power orchestration software at a NextGen Cloud data center in Montreal, Canada. According to the company, the software enabled 16 Nvidia B300 servers to operate within the power budget provisioned for ten servers. This, the company said, delivered 60 percent more nameplate compute capacity and token throughput while maintaining inference quality and reliability. Karman claimed that the technology maintained this performance under a range of workloads, including those with sustained high-power workloads. The initial partnership was announced back in March, with its stated aim to increase the available AI compute capacity within NexGen's already deployed data center footprint, maximizing its capacity in a grid-constrained environment. According to the partners, following the successful demonstration, the companies have now extended the software rollout across NexGen’s European cloud operations. “As demand for AI compute continues to accelerate, efficiency is becoming just as important as capacity. The results we’ve achieved with Karman demonstrate that we can deliver significantly more compute from our existing infrastructure without requiring additional provisioned power,” said Chris Starkey, CEO of NexGen Cloud. “This creates a compelling opportunity to improve infrastructure utilization, accelerate deployment, and ultimately deliver greater value to our customers. We’re excited to build on these results as we expand our partnership across Europe.” Karman’s platform utilizes AI to provide real-time visibility for grid operators and data center firms. It works by identifying and managing distributed energy resources, which it claims enhances resiliency and offsets the need for future infrastructure investments. The platform can integrate with smart meters, providing AI solutions for utility companies and their customers. The company developed the platform using a custom version of the Nvidia Jetson Orin Nano, an Edge AI platform, which it claims provides 100 times the processing power of other meter-based solutions. The platform can connect to millions of endpoints and coordinate them to monitor and react to real-time conditions. “The fastest, low-cost way to scale AI today is by getting more compute out of the infrastructure already built,” said Josh Brumberger, Karman CEO. “Data centers hold power in reserve for worst-case scenarios that rarely happen. Karman turns that stranded capacity into usable compute. We’re excited to bring this value to NexGen Cloud and their customers.” Karman was rebranded earlier this month, formerly operating under the name Utilidata. Also this month, the company partnered with French industrial group Legrand to integrate Karman into its data center power distribution product lines. In June, the firm raised $60.3 million in Series C funding to scale its platform, led by Renown Capital Partners, with participation from Quanta, Nvidia, and existing investor Keyframe Capital.
